🚀 About Team SHINE

We are Team SHINE, a passionate and creative team of university students from Jazan, Saudi Arabia, interested in technology, innovation, and space exploration.

Our interests include Artificial Intelligence, Web Development, Cybersecurity, Data Analysis, and creating innovative digital solutions to real-world challenges.

We believe in teamwork, creativity, and turning ideas into practical solutions. We are excited to participate in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

details:
HARRAT-X is a web platform that helps researchers judge Saudi volcanic fields (harrats) as terrestrial analog sites for Moon and Mars experiments, the goal of the challenge “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars”.

A user selects a harrat (Rahat, Khaybar, Lunayyir, Ithnayn or Al Birk). The platform shows NASA imagery, retrieves a 41-point elevation transect from NASADEM, and derives relief and slope (for Harrat Khaybar, for example, an elevation range of 643 m and a mean slope of about 1° at regional scale). The researcher then enters Moon or Mars reference values with a citation, and the platform computes a weighted similarity score, with data coverage and confidence shown next to it. A Mission Intelligence view lists what Earth cannot reproduce for each experiment, such as gravity, pressure and radiation. Results export as PDF, CSV and JSON.

Every value is labelled as measured, derived, researcher-entered or unavailable. If a reference value is missing, nothing is scored.

2) What benefits does it have?

Researchers and mission planners get a faster, more transparent way to screen candidate analog sites. Instead of a single similarity number, they see which experiments a site can support, which it cannot, what data is missing, and where each number comes from. This reduces the risk of choosing a field site for the wrong reason, and another researcher can reproduce the result from the same sources. It also works in Arabic and English.

3) What is the intended impact?

Our aim is to make analog-site selection traceable and reproducible, and to document Saudi harrats as candidate research sites for lunar and Martian surface work. Beyond research, it can serve as a teaching tool for planetary analog science. HARRAT-X is a prototype: the impact we describe is intended, and the next steps (raster-based slope, geologic maps, Landsat, PDS reference data, and LOLA/LROC lunar data) are needed before it supports real site decisions.

4) What tools did you use?

Data: NASADEM (NASA SRTM reprocessing) via OpenTopoData, NASA GIBS imagery (Blue Marble, MODIS, ASTER GDEM), NASA Trek (Mars MOLA, LRO WAC), NASA Earth Observatory references; Copernicus DEM (ESA) via Open-Meteo as a fallback.
Software: React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, Recharts, jsPDF, Supabase (authentication and storage), Vercel (hosting), GitHub.
AI: Claude (Anthropic) assisted with code and slide drafting.

5) How is your project creative?

Most analog-site comparisons produce one similarity score. HARRAT-X reframes the question from “how similar is this site?” to “what can this site actually test, and what can it not?”. Its creative features are:

  • Mission-specific results: the same site gets a different verdict for each experiment.
  • Mismatch intelligence: it states openly what Earth can never reproduce, such as Mars gravity.
  • Honest data handling: missing data lowers coverage instead of being filled in, and every value carries its source.
  • A local angle: it turns Saudi Arabia’s harrats into documented analog candidates, in an Arabic and English interface.

6) What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific validity: Earth is not Mars, so we never claim a site reproduces another planet, and we classify environmental dimensions as comparable, partially comparable, not comparable or insufficient data.
  • Data provenance: each dataset has a named source, resolution and processing method, and unintegrated datasets (Landsat, PDS, HiRISE, LOLA) are listed as planned.
  • Scale mismatch: our Earth statistics come from a regional transect, so confidence is capped and reduced when reference data has a different resolution.
  • Reproducibility and honesty: no Moon or Mars values are bundled; the researcher supplies them with a citation.
  • Accessibility: the platform opens without an account, and works in two languages.
  • Time: it was built within the 48-hour hackathon, so we prioritised a transparent method over breadth.
